It has been an exceptionally volatile earnings season:

Information Technology stocks fell -1.2% on average in October on the first trading day after reporting earnings, the weakest performance among all sectors.

This was followed by Energy and Consumer Staples, with average 1-day returns of -0.3% and -0.2%, respectively.

On the other hand, 8 out of 11 sectors recorded positive 1-day performance after reporting earnings over the same period.

Consumer Discretionary benefited the most, at +1.9%, followed by Healthcare and Industrials at +1.5% and +1.2%, respectively.

As a result, the average stock gained +0.6% on the first trading day after reporting earnings.

Tech is deviating from the rest of the market.

Americans have never been this pessimistic about their finances:

A record 41% of US consumers expect their financial situation to be worse over the next 12 months.

This figure has more than tripled since Q2 2024.

By comparison, during the 2008 Financial Crisis, this metric peaked at 23%.

This proportion is also significantly higher than in the 1970s and the 1980s, when CPI inflation was above 10%.

Furthermore, 31% of US consumers believe their personal financial situation will be worse in 5 years, double the proportion seen in the 1980s.

Americans feel as though we are in a recession.

On days like today, it's important to zoom out.

No, the AI Revolution is not "over," and the market is not "going to zero."

In fact, the Nasdaq 100 is up +11% YTD and nearly +70% since its April 2025 low.

Meanwhile, the S&P 500 is currently set to post a blended earnings +30.2% growth rate for Q3 2026.

This puts us on track for the third-straight quarter of earnings growth above 25%.

And, even after the biggest hack in crypto history, Bitcoin is down less than -5% this week.

Disruptive technologies like AI will inevitably bring heightened volatility, polarized positioning, and extreme swings in market sentiment.

However, do not let short-term volatility overshadow the broader picture.

We are in the midst of the biggest technological revolution in history.

Technical corrections are healthy, necessary, and an inevitable part of every bull market.

Do not lose sight of the bigger picture.

With bonds providing a port in the storm for now, it’s a reminder that bonds have become a viable asset class again, regardless of their sometimes-lacking anti-correlation credentials. They may not continue to be that port in the storm for long, but at least we are getting paid to take the risk (via high real yields).
